text: `Optional` is just an enum you could have written yourself.
detail: `enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none; case some(Wrapped) }` — `nil` is literally `.none`, and `String?` is sugar for `Optional<String>`. You can pattern-match one in a `switch` like any other enum.

text: `??` short-circuits like `||` does.
detail: The right-hand side of nil-coalescing is `@autoclosure`, so `expensive()` in `value ?? expensive()` only runs when `value` is actually nil.

text: Functions and closures are the same thing to the compiler.
detail: You can pass a named function anywhere a closure is expected — `items.map(String.init)` works because a function reference *is* a closure value, just one with no captures.

text: `{ $0 * 2 }` has no `return` because of implicit return.
detail: A closure whose body is a single expression returns it automatically. Swift 5.1 extended the same rule to functions and computed properties.

text: `Array`, `String`, `Dictionary` and `Set` are all structs.
detail: They achieve value semantics without copying their contents eagerly, using copy-on-write over a shared heap buffer.

text: SwiftUI's `View` is a protocol on structs, deliberately.
detail: Views are cheap values that get created and thrown away constantly. If they were classes, every diff would mean heap allocation and reference counting.

text: `Collection` declares a handful of requirements and gives you dozens of methods.
detail: `map`, `filter`, `first(where:)`, `sorted` and the rest are all protocol extension defaults written once against `startIndex`, `endIndex` and `subscript`.

text: You can conform a type you don't own to a protocol you don't own.
detail: Swift 6 wants the `@retroactive` attribute when you do, because if the owning module later adds the same conformance, which one wins is undefined.

text: ARC is a compile-time feature, not a runtime one.
detail: The compiler inserts retain/release calls while compiling. There's no background thread and no collection pause — which is why deallocation timing is predictable enough to rely on in `deinit`.

text: `weak` references are stored in a side table, not in the object.
detail: That's how every weak reference to an object can be zeroed the moment it dies, and also why reading a weak reference costs more than reading a strong one.

text: An object with unowned references pointing at it becomes a zombie, not free memory.
detail: After deinit runs, the allocation is held back while the unowned count is above zero, so accessing it traps predictably rather than reading whatever was allocated in its place.

text: `unowned(unsafe)` exists and does exactly what it sounds like.
detail: No zeroing, no unowned count, no trap — just a dangling pointer and undefined behaviour. It's for interop and hot paths, and it's the one variant worth being genuinely nervous about.

text: Xcode's memory graph debugger draws cycles for you.
detail: Pause the app, hit the memory graph button, and filter to your types — a cycle shows as a literal loop in the graph, with the offending references labelled.

text: The `weak var delegate` convention exists entirely because of retain cycles.
detail: A delegate is nearly always the delegating object's owner, so a strong delegate property would create a cycle in essentially every use.

text: `[x]` in a capture list snapshots the value at closure creation.
detail: It isn't only for `weak` and `unowned` — capturing a plain value freezes it, which is often exactly what you wanted and sidesteps lifetime questions entirely.

text: Swift 5.8 let you write `guard let self` without `= self`.
detail: Shadowing `self` was specifically allowed because the `guard let strongSelf = self` dance was so ubiquitous it warranted its own syntax.

text: The cooperative thread pool is capped at roughly the core count.
detail: That's a deliberate contrast with GCD, where every blocked queue could spawn another thread and a busy app could end up with hundreds.

text: `await` is the only place a function can suspend.
detail: Between two awaits your code runs uninterrupted within its isolation domain, which is what makes actor reasoning tractable — you only have to think about state changing at the awaits.

text: Actor reentrancy exists to prevent deadlock.
detail: If an actor stayed locked across an await, an actor awaiting something that eventually calls back into it would wait on itself forever.

text: `actor` is a reference type, like `class`.
detail: It gets identity and reference semantics — but no inheritance from other actors, and its isolated state can't be reached without going through the actor.

text: You can write your own global actor.
detail: `@globalActor actor DatabaseActor { static let shared = DatabaseActor() }` gives you a `@DatabaseActor` attribute that serialises everything marked with it, exactly like `@MainActor` does for the UI.

text: This project sets SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION to MainActor.
detail: So types are main-actor isolated by default and you opt out with `nonisolated` — the right default for an app that's mostly interface, and the reverse of what a library would want.

text: `Sendable` is a marker protocol with no requirements at all.
detail: It emits no runtime metadata — conformance exists purely so the compiler can check what crosses an isolation boundary.

text: Swift 6 turns Sendable violations from warnings into errors.
detail: Swift 5 mode with strict concurrency checking is the migration path: fix the warnings module by module, then flip the language mode.

text: `loadView` is the one method you override to replace the view entirely.
detail: Override it and don't call `super` if you're building the root view in code — but never call it yourself; touching `view` does it for you.

text: `viewDidLayoutSubviews` can run many times for a single appearance.
detail: Rotation, keyboard, split view, dynamic type and a parent's own layout can each trigger it, so it must stay cheap.

text: The keyboard-dismissing one-liner is pure responder chain.
detail: `sendAction(#selector(UIResponder.resignFirstResponder), to: nil, ...)` means "whoever is first responder, stand down" — no reference to any text field needed.

text: A presented view controller's next responder is the presenting one.
detail: The chain follows presentation and containment relationships, not just the view hierarchy, so it can jump between windows' worth of views.

text: SwiftUI recreates view structs constantly, and that's the design.
detail: They're cheap values with no heap allocation. The expensive part — the actual render tree — is kept by the framework and diffed against the new description.

text: `@State` should almost always be `private`.
detail: It's storage this view owns. If another view needs to write it, that's a `Binding`, and if the parent should own it, it belongs in the parent.

text: `Binding` stores no data — it's two closures.
detail: A getter and a setter pointing at storage owned elsewhere, which is why you can build one by hand and why it's cheap to pass around.

text: `.constant(true)` exists mostly for previews and tests.
detail: It's a binding whose setter discards writes, so you can render a view that demands a binding without wiring up real state.

text: The Observation framework isn't SwiftUI-only.
detail: `withObservationTracking(_:onChange:)` lives in the standard Observation module and works in plain Swift, including on the server.

text: `@Observable` rewrites your stored properties into computed ones.
detail: Each read calls `access(keyPath:)` and each write `withMutation(keyPath:)` against a registrar. Expanding the macro in Xcode shows exactly what it generated.
